doc.shortHtml: Reads $uri as an RFC 3986 URI reference, as parse_url does — reporting, never normalizing: every component comes back exactly as written, still percent-encoded and in its own case.

params.name: uri
params.descHtml: The text to read; a relative reference such as /a?b is accepted and answers a null scheme.

doc.returnHtml: A Uri whose readers answer the components as written.

errors.descHtml: $uri is text the RFC 3986 grammar does not admit — a space, a control byte, a non-ASCII byte, a bare % or a bracketed host that is no IPv6 address — or its authority's port is outside 0–65535. The text is not quoted back.

doc.shortHtml: Core\Uri::parse with null where it throws — the one spelling of "is this text a URI", replacing filter_var with FILTER_VALIDATE_URL; its narrower question, "is it absolute", is tryParse($s)?->scheme() != null.

params.name: uri
params.descHtml: The text to read.

doc.returnHtml: The Uri, or null for text parse would throw on — the grammar's refusals and an out-of-range port alike.

doc.shortHtml: Percent-encodes $s for use as one piece of a URI — a path segment, a fragment, one side of a query pair — as rawurlencode does: a space is %20, and every byte outside RFC 3986's unreserved set (letters, digits, -_.~) is escaped, the delimiters / ? # & = included.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to encode.

doc.returnHtml: The escaped text, with upper-case hex digits; a tainted argument comes back plain, since no byte of it can be read as a delimiter afterwards.

doc.shortHtml: Reverses Core\Uri::encodeComponent, as rawurldecode does: every %XX escape becomes its byte, and a + stays a literal +.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to decode.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded octets, as bytes — percent-decoding is defined over octets, so %FF has an answer here and text is one as string away. A malformed escape such as %G1 or a trailing % decodes to itself.

doc.shortHtml: Encodes $s as one value of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded payload — a query-string pair or a POST body — as urlencode does: a space is +, and every byte outside letters, digits and -_. is escaped, ~ and the & and = that structure a pair included.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to encode.

doc.returnHtml: The escaped text, with upper-case hex digits; a tainted argument comes back plain, since it can no longer open a pair of its own.

doc.shortHtml: Reverses Core\Uri::encodeFormValue, as urldecode does: a + is a space, %2B is a +, and every other %XX escape becomes its byte.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to decode.

doc.returnHtml: The decoded octets, as bytes, exactly as decodeComponent answers them; a malformed escape decodes to itself, and %20 reads as a space too.

doc.shortHtml: Reads a query string into an array, as parse_str does but returning it rather than populating variables: pairs split at &, each at its first =, both halves form-decoded, and PHP's bracket convention in full — a[]=1&a[]=2 builds a list, a[b]=c a map, nested to any depth.

params.name: query
params.descHtml: The query text, without its leading ?.

doc.returnHtml: An array whose every value is a bytes or a nested array<mixed> — a value is percent-decoded by the same decoder decodeFormValue is, so it answers octets; a pair without = has empty bytes for its value, a pair whose name decodes to nothing is dropped, and a repeated name without brackets keeps the last value.

errors.descHtml: A name's escapes decode to octets that are not valid UTF-8, and a name is the array key the pair is placed under, which is a string. A value has no such refusal.

doc.shortHtml: Writes $parameters as a query string, as http_build_query does — pairs joined by &, both halves form-encoded, and a nested array written under its whole bracket path with the indexes spelled out, so Core\Uri::parseQuery reads it back to the same array.

params.name: parameters
params.descHtml: The parameters: scalars, or arrays nested to any depth.

doc.returnHtml: The query text, without a leading ?; a bool is written as 1 or 0, and a null value drops its pair entirely.

errors.descHtml: A value is neither a scalar nor a nested array — an object or a closure — so there is no text to write it as.

members.name: with
members.signature: with({scheme?, host?, port?, path?, query?, fragment?}): Uri

doc.shortHtml: A fresh Uri with the named components replaced and every other one carried over, replacing reassembly by hand. Writing null for port, query or fragment removes that component, where leaving the key out carries it over; userInfo is not on the bag, so it can neither add nor drop a credential.

params.name: scheme
params.descHtml: The new scheme, without its :.

params.name: host
params.descHtml: The new host; an IPv6 literal carries its brackets.

params.name: port
params.descHtml: The new port, 0–65535, or null to remove it.

params.name: path
params.descHtml: The new path, already percent-encoded; beside a host it must begin with /.

params.name: query
params.descHtml: The new query, already encoded and without its ?, or null to remove it; "" is an empty query, which is a different thing.

params.name: fragment
params.descHtml: The new fragment, already encoded and without its #, or null to remove it.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri; the receiver is unchanged. A receiver whose port was written empty (h:/) loses that : on the way through.

errors.descHtml: port is outside 0–65535; a component makes the result text the RFC 3986 grammar does not admit; or the components do not recompose to a URI that still holds them — a path beside a host that lacks its leading / lands in the host — and the first component that moved is named.

members.name: queryParameter
members.replaces: `parse_str` over `parse_url`'s `query` key, then an array read

doc.shortHtml: One query parameter by name, read through Core\Uri::parseQuery's bracket convention instead of by parsing the query string at the call site.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The parameter's name, decoded and top-level: the brackets of a[b]=c belong to the value, so "a" is what reaches it.

doc.returnHtml: The value — bytes, or a nested array<mixed> where the convention built one — and null both for a name that is not there and for a URI with no query at all; query() is what tells those two apart.

errors.descHtml: A name in the receiver's own query decodes to octets that are not valid UTF-8, which is Core\Uri::parseQuery's refusal reached through it.

members.name: withQueryParameter
members.replaces: `parse_str`, an array edit and `http_build_query` written out at every call site

doc.shortHtml: A fresh Uri with one query parameter set, replaced or removed and every other pair carried over — Core\Uri::parseQuery, the edit and Core\Uri::buildQuery in one member instead of three at the call site.

params.name: name
params.descHtml: The parameter's name, decoded and top-level; brackets are written by an array value, never by spelling them into the name.

params.name: value
params.descHtml: The new value: a scalar, or an array nested to any depth, which is written under the bracket convention. null removes the parameter.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri; the receiver is unchanged. Removing the last parameter leaves no query at all rather than a bare ?, and every pair that is carried over is rewritten in buildQuery's spelling rather than the one it arrived in.

errors.descHtml: A name in the receiver's own query decodes to octets that are not valid UTF-8; value is neither a scalar nor a nested array; or the rebuilt reference does not still hold every component it was written out of, which is with's refusal reached through the same recompose-and-reread path.

doc.shortHtml: Resolves $reference against the receiver as a base, RFC 3986 § 5's reference resolution, which PHP has no function for: the receiver's fragment is dropped first, and dot segments are removed from the result — the one member here that rewrites a path.

params.name: reference
params.descHtml: The URI reference to resolve, relative or absolute.

doc.returnHtml: A fresh absolute Uri; the receiver is unchanged.

errors.descHtml: The receiver is a relative reference and so no base; $reference is text the RFC 3986 grammar does not admit; or the base is opaque — no authority and a rootless path, as in mailto:a@b — so there is no path to merge into.

members.name: compareTo
members.replaces: nothing — PHP compares `parse_url` arrays by hand

doc.shortHtml: Orders the receiver against $other over their RFC 3986 § 6.2.2 normal forms — Comparable's member, and the spelling of "are these the same URI": scheme and host fold to lower case, escapes' hex digits to upper, an escaped unreserved character becomes itself, and dot segments leave an absolute path. Neither side is rewritten.

params.name: other
params.descHtml: The Uri to compare against.

doc.returnHtml: -1, 0 or 1: component by component in scheme, userInfo, host, port, path, query, fragment order, an absent component before a present one. http://h:80/ and http://h/ differ — no scheme default is known.

doc.shortHtml: Answers the receiver with the reserved _sig query parameter set, over a signature taken across everything compareTo normalizes — scheme, userInfo, host, port, path and the query's parameters. Appending, removing or editing any parameter invalidates it; reordering them does not, and neither does a fragment.

params.name: settings
params.descHtml: The key ring and the lifetime, written as one literal because neither has a sensible value this member could choose.

shape.descHtml: The key ring, newest first: $keys[0] signs, and the rest exist so that a link minted before the last rotation still verifies. The same ring Core\Signature takes, and a token minted at one door does not verify at the other.

When the link stops working, inside the signed bytes where a holder cannot edit it. null is the forever spelling, and it has to be written — a permanent signed URL is a permanent bearer credential, and it ends up in browser history, Referer headers and chat unfurls.

doc.returnHtml: A new Uri, the receiver with _sig set — so it composes with with and toString like every other member here. A receiver already carrying _sig has it replaced rather than nested, and the same URL under the same key and lifetime always mints the same token. The token carries the signed form as well as the tag, so it adds about 4/3 × (URL + 40) characters. A relative reference signs without a scheme, host or port, so its token is valid on any origin: $uri->scheme() is what says which you are holding.

errors.descHtml: $settings.keys is empty, so there is no newest key; or its first entry is not 32 octets long — a bytes that was never a key.

doc.shortHtml: Checks the receiver's _sig against every key in $keys, and the lifetime that rode inside it. Answers nothing: a signed URL carries no claims to hand back — the claim is the URL the caller already holds — and a bool is a value a caller can drop.

params.name: keys
params.descHtml: The same ring sign was given, newest first. A link minted under any key still in the ring verifies; one minted under a key that has been dropped off the end does not.

doc.returnHtml: Nothing. Reaching the next statement is what says the URL is authentic and live.

errors.descHtml: $keys is empty, or one of its entries is not 32 octets long.

The URL is not one this ring signed — a parameter was added, removed or edited, the token was altered, it was minted for another door or under a retired key, there is no _sig at all, or there are two of them. Every one of those is one message. Expiry is the single refusal with a sentence of its own, because only the holder of a genuinely signed link ever reaches it.

doc.shortHtml: The scheme as written, never case-folded — parse_url's scheme key.
doc.returnHtml: The scheme without its :, or null for a relative reference.

members.name: userInfo
members.notes: one reader, not `user`/`pass` — RFC 3986 § 3.2.1 deprecates the split form
members.notesHtml: one reader, not user/pass — RFC 3986 § 3.2.1 deprecates the split form

doc.shortHtml: The whole userinfo subcomponent as written — parse_url's user and pass keys as one reader, because RFC 3986 deprecates the user:password form and a member that split it would recommend writing one.
doc.returnHtml: The text before the authority's @, still percent-encoded, or null where no @ was written.

members.name: host
members.notes: `null` where no authority was written, `""` where an empty one was
members.notesHtml: null where no authority was written, "" where an empty one was

doc.shortHtml: The host as written, never case-folded, an IPv6 literal still inside its brackets — parse_url's host key.
doc.returnHtml: The host; null where no authority was written and "" where an empty one was, as in file:///tmp.

doc.shortHtml: The authority's port as a number — parse_url's port key.
doc.returnHtml: The port, 0–65535; null where none was written and where an empty one was (http://h:/). No scheme default is ever supplied.

doc.shortHtml: The path as written, still percent-encoded and with its dot segments in place — parse_url's path key.
doc.returnHtml: The path, never null: a reference with nothing between its authority and its query has the empty path, and "" is that path.

doc.shortHtml: The raw query as written, still encoded — parse_url's query key; Core\Uri::parseQuery turns it into an array.
doc.returnHtml: The text after the ?, or null where no ? was written; a ? with nothing after it is "", not null.

doc.shortHtml: The raw fragment as written, still encoded — parse_url's fragment key.
doc.returnHtml: The text after the #, or null where no # was written; a # with nothing after it is "", not null.

doc.shortHtml: The reference this Uri was parsed from, byte for byte — not a recomposition — and what echo $uri writes.
doc.returnHtml: The original text, unchanged.

doc.shortHtml: Draws a random UUID — 122 bits from the CSPRNG under RFC 9562's version-4 layout — replacing uniqid, com_create_guid and the userland libraries around them.
doc.returnHtml: A fresh Uuid, unguessable and carrying no clock; the one to hand to a stranger.

doc.shortHtml: Draws a time-ordered UUID — a 48-bit millisecond timestamp then 74 random bits, RFC 9562's version 7 — for a database key, where an ascending identifier appends to the index instead of dirtying a random page. PHP has no equivalent.
doc.returnHtml: A fresh Uuid that sorts after every one drawn in an earlier millisecond and randomly against those drawn in the same one; its creation time is readable from it, so it is the wrong identifier to show a stranger. A host clock before 1970 is pinned to the epoch.

doc.shortHtml: Reads $s as a UUID in RFC 9562's canonical hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 form, in either letter case, replacing the hand-written validation PHP programs carried strings through.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to read, exactly 36 characters.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid those 128 bits spell; the nil and max UUIDs parse, and the version nibble is not checked.

errors.descHtml: $s is not the canonical form — the 32 unhyphenated digits, a {…}-braced spelling and a urn:uuid: prefix are refused too.

doc.shortHtml: Core\Uuid::parse with null where it throws — the one spelling of "is this text a UUID", replacing uuid_is_valid and every userland isValid.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to read.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid for the canonical hyphenated form in either case; null for anything else.

doc.shortHtml: Reads sixteen octets as a UUID — the form a native UUID column and a binary protocol carry one in, with no canonical text on the way, replacing the getBytes/fromBytes pair of the userland libraries.

params.name: b
params.descHtml: The sixteen octets, most significant first, as $uuid->toBytes() writes them.

doc.returnHtml: The Uuid those 128 bits are; every pattern is one, the nil and the max included, so a length is all this checks.

errors.descHtml: $b is not exactly sixteen bytes long; the message names the length it got.

doc.shortHtml: Renders the receiver in RFC 9562's canonical lower-case hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 form — the only way its text comes back out, and what echo $uuid writes.
doc.returnHtml: The 36-character text, lower case whatever case parse read.

doc.shortHtml: Writes the receiver's sixteen octets, most significant first — toString's twin for a native UUID column, a binary protocol or a hash input, where the canonical text would be 36 bytes spelling the same 128 bits.
doc.returnHtml: Sixteen bytes, which Core\Uuid::fromBytes reads back as this same UUID.

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether $s is an email address, as filter_var with FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL does: one @, an unquoted dot-atom local part of at most 64 bytes, and a hostname of at least two labels, at most 254 bytes in all.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for an address; false for anything else, including a quoted local part, a domain literal such as a@[192.0.2.1], a bare single-label domain and any non-ASCII byte. Nothing is looked up in DNS.

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether $s is an IP address, as filter_var with FILTER_VALIDATE_IP does, with FILTER_FLAG_IPV4 and FILTER_FLAG_IPV6 folded into version.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

params.name: version
params.descHtml: 4 or 6 to accept exactly that family; omitted, either family is accepted.

doc.returnHtml: true for an address of the chosen family; false otherwise, including an IPv4 octet with a leading zero (192.000.002.001) and an IPv6 address carrying a zone identifier (fe80::1%eth0).

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether $s is a MAC address, as filter_var with FILTER_VALIDATE_MAC does: six hex octets joined by : or by -, or three groups of four hex digits joined by ..

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for one of the three spellings in either letter case; false otherwise, including a mix of separators.

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether $s is an RFC 1123 hostname, as filter_var with FILTER_VALIDATE_DOMAIN and FILTER_FLAG_HOSTNAME does: one or more labels of 1 to 63 letters, digits and -, joined by single dots, at most 253 bytes in all.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true for a hostname, localhost and an all-numeric name included; false for a label starting or ending with -, an empty label, a trailing root dot or a byte outside ASCII. Syntax only — nothing is resolved.

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether every byte of $s is ASCII (0x00–0x7F) — the encoding question, a byte scan with no decoding.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true when no byte is above 0x7F, and true for the empty string where ctype_* answers false; false otherwise.

doc.shortHtml: Answers whether $s holds no control character — no char in Unicode general category Cc — as ctype_print does, but over characters rather than ASCII bytes, so café is printable.

params.name: s
params.descHtml: The text to test.

doc.returnHtml: true when no character is a C0 or C1 control or DEL — tab, carriage return and newline are controls and answer false — and true for the empty string. Not a spoofing check: bidirectional overrides and zero-width joiners are printable.
